sections.heading: Bidar fort
sections.content: is a fifteenth century fort which was the capital of the Bahamani dynasty. It is surrounded by a triple-moated wall, with intricate battlements and an imposing gateway. Though the ruins are crumbling the bastions and gates, royal baths and kitchens, audience halls, and pleasure pavilions stand as witnesses to Bidar's past glory. The Rang Mahal has elaborately carved wooden pillars and Persian couplets engraved in tiles and exquisite mother-of-pearl inlay work. The Solah Khambha Mosque was originally designed as a Jami masjid.

sections.heading: Karnataka- Monument- Pattadakal
sections.content: With its beautifully chiselled temples, this World Heritage Site on the banks of the Malaprabha is reminiscent of the richness of Chalukyan architecture. Pattadakal reached its glory under the Chalukya kings and was once used as a ceremonial centre where kings were crowned and commemorated. It has a cluster of ten major temples, which reflect the maturity of architectural style in the Badami and Aihole regions. At the entrance of the site, are the eight century temples of Jambulinga, Kadasiddeshvara, and Galaganatha with their curvilinear shikaras or spires. The biggest temple, dedicated to Shiva, Virupaksha, has a huge gateway, several inscriptions, and a profusion of friezes from the epics. Facing the temple is a pavilion containing a massive Nandi. The style of the large Virupaksha temple is a forerunner of the Chalukya style.This is the only temple that is still used for worship. Parts of the temple predate the Vijayanagar empire. The temple, with nine storied gopuram towers above the other structure at Hampi. The ceiling of the rangamandapa is beautifully painted with scenes from the Puranas. The Mallikarjuna Temple is similar to Virupaksha Temple, in design but smaller in size.

sections.heading: Ornate Papanatha Temple
sections.content: The ornate Papanatha Temple is yet another impressive piece of architecture, with delicately chiselled ceilings and a sixteenth pillared main hall. It has a large mandapa with a Nandi in the centre. It has a northern style shikhara. The Sangameshwara temple dating from the reign of King Vijayaditya (696-733 AD) is the earliest temple in this complex. It is built in a Dravidian style architecture similar to Pallava dynasty architecture of Kanchipuram.

sections.heading: Karnataka- Monument- Halebid
sections.content: Halebid, the ancient capital of the Hoysalas was earlier known as Dvarsamudra. The Hoysaleswara temple, perched on a star-shaped base amidst lawns, is a sculptural extravaganza. It reflects the Hoysala style in all its grandeur. Its walls are richly carved with an endless variety of Hindu deities, sages, stylised animals, birds, and friezes depicting the life of the Hoysala kings. The temple platform is carved in horizontal bands. Musicians, animals, mythical beasts and humans, have all been sculpted in a row above another band of sculptures in the same way. Even the eaves are densely carved. The tower over the vimana is broken. The temple has one Shiva shrine and another dedicated to Santaleswara, two mandapas and two Nandi shrines.

sections.heading: Karnataka- Monument- Badami
sections.content: Badami is situated at the mouth of a ravine between two rocky hills. The exquisite sculptures and the red sandstone cliffs of Badami boast of the four ancient rock-cut caves on top of a hill. They are filled with carved pillars and bracket figures. The largest of them is the third cave, dedicated to Lord Vishnu. The sculptural wonder here is the eighteen-armed Nataraja striking eighty one dance poses in the first cave overlooking the caves is the Agastya Teertha Tank. Its banks are dotted with a cluster of Bhoothanatha temples.

sections.heading: Karnataka- Monument- Aihole
sections.content: Aihole is considered as the cradle of Hindu temple architecture. There are hundreds of temples in the villages and fields nearby. Durga temple is the most impressive one with its semicircular apse, elevated plinth, and the gallery encircling the sanctum. The Ladkhan Temple, which is one of the earliest temples, was originally a royal assembly hall and marriage mandapa chosen as the abode of a Muslim prince, Lad Khan. The Huchimalli temple with a sculpture of Vishnu sitting atop a large cobra, the Ravanphadi cave temple celebrating the many forms of Shiva, the Konti temple complex, the Umamaheswari temple, the Jain Meguti Temple, and the two-storied Buddhist Temple are the other noteworthy monuments.

sections.heading: Karnataka- Monument- Lakkundi
sections.content: Lakkundi has fifty stunning temples and twenty nine inscriptions dating back to the Chalukya period. The most ornate and spectacular of these is the Kashi Vishwanatha temple. The Jain temple dedicated to Mahavira is one of the largest and oldest shrines here. Lakkundi is also noted for its step wells, artistically built with small, canopied niches inside the walls of several wells that enshrine lingas.

sections.heading: Karnataka- Monument- Bijapur-Gol Gumbaz
sections.content: The one-time capital of the Adil Shahi kings (1489-1686) is filled with mosques, mausoleums, palaces, forts, watchtowers, and strong gateways, with the massive Gol Gumbaz dominating the landscape. One of the most impressive architectural achievements of the Deccan, is the mausoleum of Muhammad Adil Shah. The tomb is set in a large walled garden, in the Persian style. This path bisects the garden. On either side are ruins of buildings made of dark bricks. This magnificent mausoleum of Mohammed Adil houses the world's second largest dome. Unsupported by pillars it is an architectural wonder. Built in 1659, its most striking features are the seven storied octagonal pillars at the four corners and the heavy bracketed cornice bellow the parapet. The Gol Gumbaz is an enormous cube of stone and masonry. The amazing whispering gallery distinctly echos the faintiest whisper eleven times.

sections.heading: Karnataka- Monument- Bijapur-Tomb of Ibrahim Rauza
sections.content: Said to have inspired the Taj Mahal in Agra the palatial Mosque and tomb of Ibrahim Rauza is very impressive. The mausoleum has a mosque and four graceful minarets within a rectangular enclosure and can be accessed by a lofty entrance tower. The mausoleum designed by Malik Sandal was surrounded by a royal garden during the Shahi rule.The facade of the mosque has five arches with elaborate plasterwork on the spandrels. The mosque has graceful arches, aisle halls, intricate designs and large crowning onion dome. This spherical dome is raised on a high neck decorated with long petals. What makes it even more special is the priceless Koran written in letters of gold that is carefully preserved here.

sections.heading: Gulbarga Fort
sections.content: The Gulbarga Fort was originally built by Raja Gulchand and later fortified by Ala-ud-din Bahman. The fort contains large buildings, mosques, temples, stables, ammunition dumps, carriages, fifteen towers, twenty six guns, and several beautiful courtyards. The most beautiful of the sprawling fort is the thirty eight thousand square feet Jumma Masjid with its elegant domes and arched columns. The crumbling ruins of Gulbarga Fort, the Sultan Hasan's tomb, the tomb of Ghias-ud-din, the fine mausoleum of Feroze Shah and family, the Haft-Gumbaz reminds one of Karnataka's glorious past, when kingdoms fell and others rose from their ashes.

sections.heading: Mysore Palace
sections.content: The original Mysore palace built of wood, got burnt down in 1897 and was rebuilt for the twenty fourth Wodeyar king in 1912. Designed by the well-known British architect, Henry Irwin, the palace is a treasure house of exquisite carvings. Built in Indo-Saracenic style with domes, turrets, arches, and colonnades, the Mysore palace is a treasure house of works of art from all over the world. Intricately carved doors open into luxuriously furnished rooms. The majestic Durbar hall has an ornate ceiling and many sculpted pillars. The marriage pavilion is adorned with glazed tile flooring, stained glass windows and domed ceilings. The walled palace complex houses the residential museum, temples, and shrines, including the Shwetha Varahaswamy temple. The magnificently jewel-studded golden throne, the

sections.heading: Karnataka- Monument- Somnathpur
sections.content: Situated in the village of Somnathpur, the exquisitely carved, star-shaped temple with triple towers is a perfect example of Hoysala architecture. This place boasts of one of the last and the grandest of Hoysala monuments - the Kesava temple. By the year 1268 CE, the year in which the Kesava temple at Somnathpur was built. The riches and splendour of the Hoysala court were already evident in their grand temples at Belur and Dvarasamudra (present day, Halebid). The Hoysala temple at Somnathpur, is truly unique in design, perfect in proportion and the stone carvings are striking marvels in stone. The shrine stands in the centre of a walled compound, around which runs an open verandah with sixty four cells. The temple itself, stellar in shape, has three elaborately carved pinnacles with a common Navranga and stands on a raised platform. The three sanctums once housed beautifully carved idols of Kesava, Janardhana and Venugopala. Today the idol of Lord Kesava is missing, but the other two still adorn the sanctums in their original form. The friezes on its outer walls with their intricately carved rows of elephants, charging horsemen, and mythological birds and beasts leaves one spellbound. Beautifullysculpted images of gods, goddesses, and scenes from the epics, as well as the remarkably ornate ceilings in the pillared hall are very beautiful. At the temple, the outer walls are decorated with a series of star-shaped folds and the entire surface is covered with carved stone plaques. The walls above the plinth are also carved with exquisite figures of gods and goddesses, taken from the Hindu puranas, and meticulously arranged in vertical panels.

sections.heading: Karnataka  Monument- Shravanbelagola
sections.content: Shravanbelagola, is one of the most important Jain pilgrim centres of India. The statue of the Jain saint Gommateshwara (981 CE) is one of the tallest and most graceful statues in the world. It is carved out of a mountain and is situated in the Indragiri hills. The colossal monolithic statue is fifty eight feet high, with twenty six ft wide shoulders, ten feet of its feet. Starkingly simple, the beautifully chiseled features of this statue embody serenity. Nearly 1,800 years old, the statue which is reached by climbing seven hundred steps carved in the steep granite slope, is symbolic of the renunciation of worldly possessions. It was sculpted by Aristanemi in 981 CE and Chamunda Raya, a general and minister of the Ganga King Rachamatta installed it in 983 CE. Lord Gomatesheshwara was the Jain prince Bahubali. During a war with his greedy elder brother, Bharata who wanted to grab the kingdom, Bahubali accepted defeat at the moment of his victory when he realized the futility of it all. He renounced the world and left to lead a life of penance and meditation, attaining nirvana. Thousands of devotees congregate here to perform the Mahamastakabhisheka. It is a spectacular ceremony which is the focus for Jain pilgrims across India, held once in twelve years. Hundreds of pots containing curds, milk, honey, vermilion, coconut water, turmeric paste and even gold and precious jewels are poured over the statue's head by priests. In addition to the statue, there are several Jain temples and monasteries in Shravanabelagola and it attained historical importance when Chandragupta Maurya, the greatest King of Mauryan Empire, settled on this hill in third century BCE, along with his Guru Bhagwan Bhadra Bahu Swami, after renouncing his kingdom.

sections.heading: Karnataka  Museum - Tipu Sultan Museum
sections.content: Established in 1959, in memory of Tipu Sultan and Tipu Sultan museum is an archeological museum situated at Srirangapatna which preserves many historic items and personal belongings of Tipu and his family. The museum is housed in the Dariya Daulat Khana, a summer palace of Tipu Sultan. The museum is constructed mainly in wood and the structure rests on a vast plinth. The walls and ceilings of the building are elaborately painted. The murals on the outer walls depict scenes from Tipu's wars while the interior walls are ornately painted with abstract designs and floral motifs. The museum showcases sketches of Tipu, Hyder Ali, Srirangapatna fort, Srirangapatna from different angles and Bangalore during that period. The alcove carrying the portraits and charcoal drawings of Tipu and his family is the major attraction. Also on display are a number of maps of Tipu's forts and his dominions, the coinage used during the reigns of Tipu and Hyder Ali, and medals awarded by Tipu.

sections.heading: Karnataka-Handicrafts- Chennapatna
sections.content: Chennapatna is well known for its unusual wooden lacquered toys and products. These craftsmen called chitragars are involved in this traditional craft since ages and make beautiful toys like a grinding stone, mortar, pestle and rolling pin, as well as a well to hold water. Other creations include Wood turning requires extremely close grained and moderately hard wood and Hale wood is the most suited wood found in this region. The required size and shape of wood is cut, seasoned, attached on to a lathe and turned in order to smoothen it. Chisels are used to shape the revolving piece of wood and flaws are sandpapered away with. The lacquering of the surface is done by rubbing lac sticks into the revolving wood and imprinting it with lacs in reds, yellows, greens, blacks and mauve. Plain lacquering is favoured though abri or cloud work, zig-zags, stripes, and dana or the spotted technique are also used.

sections.heading: Karnataka- Handicrafts- Sandalwood Carving
sections.content: Karnataka has a huge forest-belt and sandalwood carvers are found in Bangalore, Mysore, Shimoga, Honavar and Kumta on the coast. Sandalwood is of great religious importance and is an extremely expensive material for carving artifacts. Sandalwood is of two types: srigandha which is close grained and yellowish-brown in colour and used for carving; and nagagandha which is darkish-brown in colour and from which oil is extracted. Sandalwood is a rich, golden brown wood that gives off a fragrance. The wood is cultured and used to make a plethora of products that range from idols of deities and finely twisted chariots to decorative pieces such as paper cutters, walking sticks, trays, boxes and elephant figures. Jali or fret work with patterns in high and low relief are generally seen on them.

sections.heading: Karnataka  Handicrafts - Agarbatti/Incense Stick Making
sections.content: Incense stics or agarbatti hold the base of bamboo and the top coating over the stick is a blend of aromatic herbs derived from nature. The incense sticks have a religious significance as they are lit during the prayers and festivals. Today people use them as mood enhancers as the soothing fragrance relaxes the muscles. It is also utilized during the aromatherapy. Most of the fragrances are chemical free as they are blend of the natural aromatic herbs. Sandalwood is a popular source for agarbattis. The wood pulp of Sandalwood remaining after oil extraction still retains some aroma. It is made into a paste and wrapped around thin bamboo canes, to be burnt as incense.

sections.heading: Karnataka- Handicrafts- Rosewood/ Wood Carving Inlay work
sections.content: Mysore and Bangalore are the main centers for rosewood carving and artists make beautiful decoration and utility objects from this. There are temples and palaces which have ancestral art of wood carving on the bracketed pillars, door frames and arches. Rosewood furniture and elephants fitures are the products which are always in high demand. Wood inlay is the process of decorating the surface of wood by setting in pieces of material such as ivory, bone, plastic, or wood of different colours. This craft is also concentrated in Mysore and Bangalore where its roots can be traced back to a family by the name of Mirza Yusuf Ali who was pioneer in the field. The artisan smoothens the base of the rosewood and the design is traced and etched into the surface. The several components of the inlay are painstakingly assembled to match and fit exactly into the grooves and are then glued in. The design is finished by obtaining the required shades with several coats of polish. Examples of some famous inlay work in Karnataka include the ivory inlay in rosewood and ebony in the Srirangapatnam mausoleum; the doors of the Amba Vilas palace in Mysore are also fine examples of inlay. Products with inlay include plates, boxes, bowls, cigarette cases, and figures of animals, especially elephants, which continue to be popular. The designs include floral and geometric patterns, landscapes, pastoral scenes, processions, and scenes from the epics.

sections.heading: Interesting Facts
sections.content: In Karnataka, the puppet theatre is said to have existed since ancient times. The two prominent forms of puppetry in the state are string puppets or Marionettes and Leather or Shadow puppets. At present many marionette troops exist in Karnataka in which the whole family works as a team. A string puppet means a puppet manipulated from above and controlled by long strings invisible to the audience. Made of wood, the puppets of North Karnataka are short and slim in appearance possessing a pair of legs and hands whereas the puppets of south Karnataka are three feet high but without legs. All puppets are controlled by strings and the strings are tied to the hands and the head of the puppet. Some of the puppet troupes have discarded strings and have replaced them with rods for easier manipulation of puppets.The usually consisting of a thick black backdrop, two or three wooden poles and a curtain to cover the puppet players from being seen by the audience. Prominent musical instruments used during the performance are mridangam (also known as Maddale in Kannada), mukhaveena (a unique wind instrument made of wood, measuring one feet long and consisting twelve holes), cymbals and a Harmonium. The puppeteers of Karnataka perform the dual role of a narrator and an operator simultaneously. They not only manipulate the puppets behind the curtains but also conduct dialogues. The puppet operator wear anklets and dance along with puppets but such actions are not visible to the audience. Leather puppetry is an ancient art which existed in the third century in Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh. At present, the leather puppetry is extensively found in Chitradurga, Bellary and Kolar districts. The puppeteers following this art are known as Gomberamas or Killekyatas. These troupes numbering forty are the only nomadic clan practicing this profession. The striking feature of shadow puppetry is that, they create a world of fantasy and colour just behind the screen. Their uniqueness lies in their shadow performance. In reality, in such a show, the actual puppet is concealed behind a screen and only its shadow is visible to the audience, requiring enormous skills to present a shadow puppet show. The leather puppets are made of either goat or deer skin which is painted with vegetable dyes. The leather puppets are flat structures and are transparent. The arms, legs and head of the puppet are movable. The musical narration is simple and vivid. The puppet show requires a simple stage. A white screen is important since it is behind this that the puppets are played and on which shadows of the performing puppets are cast. The puppeteers hide themselves from the audience's view behind a thick black blanket. A lamp is hung behind the white screen. The reflection of the light falls on the puppets whose shadows ultimately appear on the transparent white cotton screen.

sections.heading: Karnataka- Performing Art- Yakshagaana
sections.content: Yakshagaana is believed to have a history of one thousand years and is believed to represent a specific type of music of the yakhas. Yaksha are the demi-gods attending on 'Kubera'- the god of wealth in the Hindu mythology. Gaana means song. By combining the meaning, the term Yakshagaana might mean the 'song of Yakshas'. Of the twenty districts in Karnataka, Yakshagana has established its firm roots in the districts of Dakshina Kannada, Uttara Kannada, Dharwad, Mysore and Hassan. The epics of Ramayana and Mahabharata offer extensive material for Yakshagana prasangas (or themes). The literature is presented both in verse and prose and the former is interpreted in simple prose and dialogues. The show begins with an announcement of Yakshagana by beating the drum, in important places of the village. Yakshagana is performed in a rectangular stage built with four wooden poles installed on four corners and covered by mats of palm leaves on the top. Away from the backstage is a small place called 'chowki', the greenroom for the artistes. The audience sits on all the three sides of the platform and a curtain covers only the back stage. In the Yakshagana , the Bhagavata is the chief narrator of the story, who recites it in verse form. Bhagavata also conducts light hearted conversation with the Vidushaka- the jester. The dialogues between these two characters is very amusing and the Bhagavata ably supports the Vidushaka in carrying out extempore dialogues. Music is the essence of Yakshagana and the narration is in verse form. It is the songs and poems which transmit the story and the songs are invariably sung by the Bhagavata. The music is excellent and synchronizes well with the costume and make up of the characters. Prose in Yakshagana is in the form of dialogues. The songs sung by the Bhagavata are at a very high pitch and hence is considered as a distinct style of music. The rhythm that dictates the body movements, footwork and the performance actually flows from the musical instruments.

sections.heading: Mysore Palace
sections.content: Although Dussera is celebrated all over India, it has special significance in Mysore. Dussera-ravana-kolam as it is called, is celebrated for ten days to symbolize the victory of goddess Chamundeswari (Durga) over the demon Mahishasura. i.e. the victory of the good over the evil. Mysore palace is fully illuminated for a whole month. On the last day, bands accompanied by a colourfully bedecked elephant carrying the statue of the goddess starts from the palace as a procession with palace chariots and units of the army through the city to Banni mandap (where Banni tree is worshipped. In the evening, there is a torchlight parade and a great display of fireworks. The magnificent ruined city of Hampi, which was once the capital of the Vijayanagar Empire was considered one of the greatest empires in the history of India. Vijayanagara became most powerful during the reigns of Krishnadevaraya and Achyutadevaraya when opulent palaces, marvellous temples, massive fortifications, baths, markets, aquaducts, pavilions, stables for royal elephants, and elegantly carved pillars were all built. This was a city whose merchants offered diamonds, pearls, fine silks, brocades and horses. This was also the period of greatest architectural activity, as both these rulers commissioned several buildings in the royal capital and in other parts of their vast empire. Most of the sites were early sixteenth century, during the twenty year reign of Krishna Deva Raya (1509 -1529). It has ruins of stone temples, elephant stables, barracks and palaces. Temples of this city are noted for their large dimensions, florid ornamentation, bold and delicate carvings, stately pillars, magnificent pavilions etc. Some of the beautiful monuments in Hampi are made out of a brilliant mix of the Hindu and Islamic style of architecture, popularly called as the Indo- Sarasenic architecture. This World Heritage Site has two important sites the royal Centre and the Sacred Centre. The Royal centre contains structures that seem to have been palaces, baths, pavilions, royal stables, and temples for ceremonial use. The Sacred Centre is situated on the northern edge of the city along the banks of the holy Tungabhadra river. The Queens bath which is a plain looking building from outside has an elaborate interior with a giant tank at the center. The corridor around has arches, domes and balconies which makes it look more like a palatial structure than a bath. The Kings Palace is the largest and includes two major structures an underground chamber which must have served as a treasury or private audience platform has densely carved bands of horses, soldiers and depiction of the various aspects of courtly life. Hazara Rama Temple was a royal temple. The entire temple is embellished with bas-reliefs depicting the scenes from the Ramayana. The walls are richly carved with friezes depicting processions of horses, elephants, dancing girls and soldiers attired in splendid weaponry. Vithala Temple in Hampi has a magnificent stone chariot standing in the temple courtyard with an equally impressive rangamandapa with fifxty six musical pillars that resound the musical chimes when struck.
